summary: Strong salary and benefits but toxic management environment
pros: When it comes to salary and benefits, I can proudly say that GM really exceeded my expectations.
cons:
I had been with GM for several years, and I never imagined reaching a point where my work environment would affect me so much, both physically and mentally.

One of the most difficult parts of my experience was dealing with a particular lead whose management style had a significant impact on me. I felt that there was very little room for mistakes or vulnerability. Some statements that were repeatedly emphasized to me were, “There is no room for mistakes here. If you can’t do it, there are a lot of companies out there,” and “Pray ka na lang.” Those words may have been intended differently, but for me, they were extremely discouraging and painful, especially during a time when I was already struggling.

I was very open about the areas where I was having difficulty, and I was never afraid to ask for help. I was told that I could reach out whenever I needed assistance. However, whenever I asked questions, I often felt that instead of receiving guidance, I was given another question and expected to figure everything out on my own. I was willing to learn and improve, but there were times when I genuinely needed direction and support.

Over time, I started feeling that almost everything I did was being questioned. Even during meetings, I would sometimes leave feeling embarrassed, discouraged, and doubtful of my own abilities. There were situations where nothing was directly said, but the way certain conversations and interactions happened made me feel inadequate and as though I was not capable of doing my job.

This experience took a significant toll on me. I experienced a level of stress and emotional exhaustion that I had never experienced throughout my career. I was never medically diagnosed with depression, but I knew that something was wrong because I could feel the impact on me physically and mentally. I reached a point where I no longer felt like myself.

I believe mistakes are part of learning, and accountability is important in any workplace. However, employees also need proper guidance, communication, patience, and respect. Telling someone that there is no room for mistakes may create fear rather than encourage growth. Asking for help should not make an employee feel stupid, incapable, or ashamed.
advice:
Some leaders seem more focused on achieving a “perfect” team score than on understanding the actual people behind those numbers. A team is made up of human beings, not just metrics and performance scores. Napromote lang, pero parang kailangan perfect ang team at walang puwedeng magkamali. Leadership should not be about protecting a score at the expense of people’s well-being.

I also hope the company takes a closer look at workplace culture. Employees should not have to deal with performative or “plastic” behavior just to survive in the workplace. Recognition, bonuses, and performance rewards should not be the only things that matter. What about how people are treated along the way?

I sincerely hope GM takes employee feedback seriously, especially when it comes to leadership. Please validate the people you put in leadership positions—not just their numbers and performance, but also how they treat the people they lead. LPZA

There were a lot of poor decisions made when it came to new extensions of the business (aka Maven, Lyft, Bright Drop, Cruise, etc), and unfortunately the senior leadership who made those decisions did not face any consequences. It was the individual contributors that took the hit. The Mountain View location is likely a fleeting trend that will be retired (a la Cadillac in New York) and the significant stock buybacks have impacted a lot of legacy employees. These decisions are designed to inflate stock prices, but it's simply not sustainable. I'm very sad that I had to leave because the culture was once fantastic, but now it's poor and creates constant fear.
advice: Please reconsider the current HR administration, and hold the senior leaders (aka decision makers) more accountable for poor investment decisions.

summary: Disappointing internship with unclear publication process
pros: Flexable for Remote and In-person
cons:
My experience as a PhD Research Intern was disappointing, particularly as someone who joined expecting a publication-oriented research internship.

The internship was 12 weeks long. From the beginning, my mentor set the expectation that the project should reach “best-quality work at ICLR” level and monitored progress very aggressively. On some days, I received more than ten Slack messages asking for updates.

About halfway through the internship, I was told that there would be no extension, so the entire project had to be completed end-to-end within the remaining ~6 weeks. At the same time, I was told that submitting the work to a workshop was not an option. This effectively created a full-conference-paper-or-nothing situation within a very short internship.

I worked hard to finish the experiments and produced a full paper draft. After submitting it internally, I was then told that it needed another internal review to determine whether the work was “worth publishing.”

This was separate from the normal IP/legal/confidentiality review that I expected at an industry research lab.

I asked how long this review would take but did not receive a clear timeline.

Before offboarding, I was asked to organize and hand over all model checkpoints, code, benchmark logs, and model outputs. By the time I returned my laptop, I still did not know:

how long the internal publication review would take,
whether the work would ultimately be approved for publication,
or whether I would be allowed to continue improving the paper after the internship.

I completely understand that industry research requires confidentiality and internal publication review. The problem was the combination of an extremely ambitious publication target, no extension, no workshop option, and an open-ended publication approval process without a clear timeline or criteria.

For PhD students whose main reason for doing a research internship is to produce publishable academic work, I would recommend getting the publication policy, review timeline, extension policy, and post-internship publication process clarified in writing before accepting an offer.

My experience reflects one team and should not be interpreted as representing every research group at GM.

summary: Strong Compensation and Remote Flexibility, but Leadership and Culture Are Misaligned
pros: Competitive salary, remote work flexibility, and decent benefits made the company an attractive place to work despite its organizational challenges.
cons:
In my experience, the company’s stated values and the culture employees actually experience are often very different. One of the biggest issues I observed was cronyism. Hiring, promotions, and career opportunities often seemed to be based more on who people knew than on performance, qualifications, or the work they actually produced.

It wasn’t unusual to see groups of employees who had worked together at previous companies, including former managers and direct reports, former coworkers, mentor-mentee relationships, and even husband-and-wife teams. While hiring people you know isn’t automatically a bad thing, it became hard to ignore how often these connections seemed to influence decisions. Many of these relationships appeared to come from the same legacy company, which created the impression that if you weren’t already part of that network, you were at a disadvantage.

If you’re looking for a workplace where your work speaks for itself and advancement is based on merit, this may not be the environment you’re expecting. It often felt like relationships carried more weight than results, and that made it difficult to believe the company’s messaging about its culture.

Leadership also seemed more interested in recreating the structure and way of doing things from legacy insurance companies than building something new. Too many decisions reflected outdated ways of thinking instead of adapting to today’s business environment. In my opinion, that held the company back, hurt morale, and kept it from becoming the kind of workplace it claimed it wanted to be.

summary: Toxic culture overshadowed by fear and forced rankings
pros: In the past GM was a great place to work.  How do I know this?  I was there for 30+ years and just retired this year.
cons:
Forced rankings and the annual dismissal of 10–15% of employees have created a toxic culture. What was once an open, collaborative environment where people worked together for the good of the company has shifted into one where employees protect their work and focus on staying in the top percentiles. This process has been in place for 5+ years, and it is reasonable to assume that any true underperformance was addressed in most departments during the first couple of cycles. At this point, the system feels less like a performance tool and more like a popularity contest. Managers are placed in impossible positions by leadership and forced to make difficult decisions about their teams.
Workplace of Choice culture survey scores may appear to be improving, but the reality is more complicated. Employees are afraid to give honest negative feedback because they believe they may be targeted afterward—and unfortunately, that fear is justified. I have sat in HR meetings where the focus was not on addressing the feedback itself, but on trying to determine who made the negative comments. The stated reason was so that person could be “coached,” yet those individuals often seem to disappear in the next forced ranking cycle.
Finally, AI is being overused in ways that create more activity without adding meaningful value. It is generating additional work that then gets stuck at existing choke points, increasing the appearance of “work completed” without improving outcomes.
advice:
Forced ranking should be eliminated immediately and the senior leader who brought it in should be fired. 
Quit believing anything coming in from Workplace of Choice culture survey is relevant.  Lost productivity on the current process is tremendous.

summary: Extremely poor management and leadership
pros:
Some good technical exposure.
Opportunities to work on enterprise-scale infrastructure and SRE/DevOps projects.
cons:
The biggest issue was management and leadership. My experience with the lead was extremely negative.

There was a lack of clear direction, ownership, and consistent expectations. Requirements could change after the work was completed, and decisions that had previously been discussed or agreed upon were later questioned.

For example, I was given a dashboard assignment. Based on my experience, I designed the dashboard and presented the complete approach. I was then asked to remove one particular item, which I did and communicated through email. Later, I was questioned about why that item had been removed.

A similar situation happened with a Grafana UAT-to-Production alert migration. I designed and implemented a pipeline based on the approach that had been discussed and agreed upon. During the final demo, instead of focusing on the delivered solution, I was questioned about why I had implemented it that way and why I had not connected earlier. I referred back to the Jira discussion showing that the approach had previously been communicated.

These situations created a pattern where expectations were unclear, decisions were not consistently maintained, and accountability appeared to fall on the engineer even when the approach had previously been discussed.

Most concerning was the lack of constructive performance feedback and clear expectations. Issues should be discussed openly during the work so employees have an opportunity to correct them, rather than being surprised by negative feedback later.

I have also seen another colleague experience a very similar situation, which makes me concerned that this may be a broader management issue rather than an isolated incident.

Management needs significant improvement in communication, requirement clarity, consistency, and fair performance management.
advice: Improve leadership accountability and communication. Clearly define expectations before assigning work, document decisions, provide timely feedback, and avoid changing expectations after delivery. Employees should have a fair opportunity to understand and address performance concerns before serious action is taken.

Competitive salary (starting at 65k)
Commission opportunities (based on performance)
Comprehensive benefits, including medical, dental, vision, pet insurance, and tuition reimbursement

Weekly pay
Wellness programs
cons:
In my experience, HR was not accommodating when I requested support for a documented medical condition.
Physically demanding work requiring constant lifting, stocking, and movement—often handling 200+ cases per shift.
Many long-tenured employees experience significant wear and tear on their bodies, particularly knee and back problems (some needing severe surgeries like spinal cord and knee replacement).

Poor work-life balance.

Strict attendance policy, with limited flexibility for unexpected absences.
Frontline employees often feel undervalued and replaceable.
Training is inconsistent despite extremely high performance expectations.
Limited opportunities to transition from Route Sales into corporate positions, even with relevant education and experience.
The company often appears to prioritize external hires over experienced internal employees for leadership positions.
Delivery trucks can have mechanical issues, raising safety concerns.
Very limited time to take meal breaks during shifts.
Trucks are often not cleaned regularly.
Employees may be expected to work during severe weather conditions, creating additional safety concerns.

Invest more in your frontline employees—they are the backbone of the business. Create clearer pathways for internal promotion into leadership and corporate roles, and prioritize developing employees who have demonstrated performance, experience, and commitment to the company. Improve the consistency and quality of training so expectations align with the support provided.

Review workloads, scheduling practices, and route expectations to better support work-life balance and reduce burnout. Ensure delivery vehicles are properly maintained and cleaned, and continue evaluating safety protocols for severe weather conditions. Finally, foster a culture where HR is viewed as a true partner by providing consistent support for employees, including those requesting reasonable workplace accommodations.

summary: your experience will depend heavily on the leadership you report to
pros: My early years at the company were genuinely strong — smart colleagues, meaningful analytical work, and leaders who understood both the technical and business context. Those years set a high bar for what the culture could be.
cons:
In more recent years, leadership turnover introduced managers who lacked the technical grounding needed to define roles, evaluate work, or provide stable direction. As a result, priorities shifted frequently, expectations changed without explanation, and roles expanded quietly to absorb whatever gaps emerged. Much of the decision making moved into the hands of leaders who were uncomfortable engaging with technical detail, which led to misaligned goals, avoidable rework, and a growing reliance on formal processes instead of straightforward conversations. This created an environment where strong contributors spent more time navigating ambiguity than doing meaningful work.
Job descriptions often read like a historical list of everything the previous person touched rather than a coherent, well scoped role. Candidates should be aware that posted responsibilities may not reflect the actual expectations once inside the team. Advice to Candidates: Ask very specific questions about how priorities are set, how often responsibilities change, and how success is measured. Clarify who will be defining your work and how much technical understanding they bring to that role.
advice: Provide leaders with the technical support and communication training needed to set clear expectations and engage directly with their teams. Overreliance on process in place of conversation erodes trust and drives away experienced talent.

summary: Meh.
pros:
Salaried employees are compensated pretty well compared to industry averages, at least in my experience. There are often opportunities to move around a lot internally. Benefits are decent enough compared to other companies (used to be better but have been going downhill with the new CEO and all the company's recent financial setbacks).

If you need a job, there are much worse options here in America (sadly...), which is about the best I can say.
cons:
You're working for a bloodsucking corporation, at least in the eyes of most Americans. If you have a conscience/a soul, working here will eat away at you the more exposed you are to what UHG cares most about (making profit line go up, giving big comp packages to upper management, and maintaining the status quo at all costs--NOT "making the health system work better for everyone"). 

The recent cuts to benefits, the forced RTO policy, the many rounds of layoffs, and the no-raises of the last couple years (plus the many high-profile lawsuits, the Change Healthcare disaster, etc.) speak for themselves: you're expendable and the company doesn't care who it hurts in its relentless pursuit of ever-growing profit. This is especially true now that UHG is pushing AI for everyone and everything. They will not hesitate to automate your job (they asked an employee to "train the AI agent," then laid them off 2 weeks after improvements were offered and training finished).

Corporate has some good people and, unfortunately, a whole lot of bad apples (catty types who believe in rules for thee but not for me). It's a low-trust, high-anxiety environment, and it definitely feels like most people just work there for the money. Disruptive thinkers are not really encouraged or rewarded. People advance by sucking up to the right leaders and ruthlessly outmaneuvering rivals. Think Game of Thrones.

If you have other options, think long and hard before you come to work here.
advice: I will not waste my time offering advice to those who refuse to listen. But maybe try treating others the way you'd want to be treated... AI will come for YOUR jobs too someday.

summary: Good Pay, Poor Leadership: A Disappointing Employee Experience
pros: Good compensation, supportive Call Quality team, helpful colleagues, remote flexibility
cons: Disorganized training and campaigns, poor leadership, inconsistent communication, inadequate coaching, unreliable technology, unfair performance metrics, excessive productivity pressure, constantly changing expectations
advice:
Invest in better training, coaching, technology, leadership accountability, campaign planning, and the overall tiering system. When new campaigns, processes, or requirements are introduced, agents should be given structured time off the phones to learn, practice, and prepare. It is contradictory to prioritize call productivity while expecting agents to immediately implement new processes without adequate preparation time.

The campaign process itself needs significant improvement. Too often, new campaigns seemed to be introduced without a clear script, structured call flow, or fully developed strategy. Agents were expected to “figure it out” while actively taking calls, and then asked for ideas about how the campaign could work better. Soliciting agent feedback is a good idea, but that feedback needs to be incorporated into the process before agents are expected to perform. It was frustrating to see improvements sometimes take days to materialize, particularly when a more experienced agent eventually created a script or approach based on their own experience that could have been provided from the beginning.

I also believe the tiering system needs to be reevaluated. Tier placement should accurately reflect an employee’s actual performance and should account for factors outside of the employee’s control, including misrouted calls, technical problems, system issues, and campaign-related challenges. Employees should not be automatically disadvantaged by a campaign or operational issue simply because of their existing tier.

Finally, the hiring and team-placement process could be improved. Supervisors should not have excessive discretion over which employees are placed on their teams without appropriate consideration of leadership effectiveness and employee fit. New employees deserve leaders who are prepared to communicate, coach, and support them.

Humana has employees who genuinely want to succeed, but they need organized campaigns, clear scripts and expectations, adequate training time, reliable technology, a fair tiering system, and leadership that is actually available when support is needed.

summary: Toxic culture with unrealistic expectations and poor pay
pros: Would not recommend to anyone.
cons:
While working from home sounds appealing, my experience at Humana felt more like being chained to my desk. In my experience, I was expected to notify my manager if I stepped away for just a couple of minutes to use the restroom or get water, and there was a heavy emphasis on monitoring productivity as they monitor your keyboard strokes.

The job often felt like a nurse production line, with expectations that seemed unrealistic and metrics that, in my opinion, prioritized volume over quality patient care. Mandatory overtime became the norm for months at a time, making work-life balance extremely difficult.

One of the biggest disappointments was compensation. At year-end, employees were told they would not receive raises because a bonus had been paid. To me, a bonus should recognize exceptional performance, not replace an annual raise that helps keep pace with increased responsibilities and the cost of living.

My experience with middle management was also very negative. I found the leadership to be unsupportive, and the workplace culture often felt toxic. Frequent reminders that our jobs were at risk created unnecessary stress, contributed to burnout, and made it difficult to feel valued as an employee.

I also personally experienced what I believed to be unfair treatment related to race and team assignments. Additionally, when I resigned, I discovered that part of my final time had not been included on my paycheck. In my experience, approval for correcting the issue was delayed, intentionally by my manager which postponed receiving my full final pay.

Overall, I would not recommend this employer based on my experience. If you’re looking for a nursing role that emphasizes autonomy, professional judgment, and work-life balance, this was not that environment.

We have enough to deal with getting our patients correct medications in record time, we don't need Humana the company shoving stuff down our throats when we just want to take care of our patients. Nobody cares what anyone looks like, leave us out of the company madness that is constant Humana DEI indoctrination.

A Warning About Toxic Management Culture

Too much control is given to managers, to the point where some start believing they own your time, your availability, and even your career.

You are expected to answer calls at any time, constantly prove your worth, and accept “feedback” and “evaluation” that often have no measurable criteria behind them. When KPIs are vague—such as “keep taking feedback from the GCC manager and help him with anything he needs”—it becomes impossible to objectively measure performance. It also creates an environment where your willingness to do unlimited work can be mistaken for performance.

What is even more frustrating is watching employees do the actual work while managers take ownership of the outcomes. It can feel less like development and more like an open transfer of credit.

The most disappointing part is that organizations can attract people by offering compensation above the market, but money alone cannot compensate for an environment that continuously drains you, limits your growth, and makes you question your own capabilities.

I genuinely feel that I have lost some of the expertise and professional confidence I had built before joining this organization, because instead of being challenged to grow, I have spent too much energy navigating politics, proving myself, and dealing with unnecessary managerial pressure.

If you are considering joining a company like this, look beyond the salary package. Ask about the actual KPIs, career progression, decision-making authority, learning opportunities, manager expectations, and how performance is objectively measured.

A higher salary is not always a better opportunity.

Sometimes, they pay you more because there is very little else they can offer you.

And no matter how much you deliver, if the culture is built around control rather than growth, your manager may keep moving the goalposts and making you feel like you are never good enough.

Protect your expertise. Protect your peace. And don't sacrifice long-term career growth for a salary number.

So for the meantime while I pursue this I thought it almost mandatory to let other people know so this behavior isn't seen as acceptable. Other than that the crew has been nothing but amazing. My first day is coming up soon so we shall see if they retaliate to my report and if so that'll just go straight to my lawyer for more evidence. summary: All Aboard the Sinking Ship!
pros:
Firstly, the vast majority of reviews on here are not from people who work for subway. Subway employs only a few hundred people, everyone who works in a restaurant works for an independent franchisee, not Subway.

That being said, Subway is a relaxed, but depressing place to work. In the past, there was real financial incentive to work here, but beware of new salary freezes and missed bonuses. The office is quite nice, the benefits are average, and the location is solid. I would not recommend new employees join unless you're getting a title upgrade and significantly more money. The people here are generally talented and intelligent, so you're working with high quality professionals, they don't hire anyone out of school.
cons: The business is in shambles and will absolutely shrink long term (think of a slower Quiznos decline). The C suite has been swapped out every couple years or so this decade, and none of them are capable of mounting a turnaround. Frankly, until underperforming franchisees are closed en-masse, the business will continue to get worse and worse. For you as an employee, this means no wages and no bonus. And money should really be your only reason for working here, as there's no culture or extraordinary benefits to speak of (and no, no free sandwiches for employees.) Internal promotions are scarce, and there isn't an established framework to get one. The US focused team has lost probably half its people in the past 8 months - half were fired and half quit. Anyone who has been here longer for a year is generally looking for a way out. There are strict limits on spending, so don't expect to be full funded or to have growing headcount. Most teams are shrinking or holding, and you may be about to replace a long time employee who recently got fired. I'd seriously reconsider working here if you're looking at a lateral move title or money wise. Things will continue to get worse for the foreseeable future.

summary: Poor Management, Favoritism, and Unrealistic Expectations
pros: Consistent weekly scheduling, employee merchandise, 30 minute lunch breaks with an employee meal, and a clean environment. A fast-paced environment for those who work well under pressure.
cons:
Working here was one of the most challenging employment experiences I've had, largely due to poor management and unrealistic expectations placed on employees.

The workplace operated with a constant sense of disorder. Employees were often required to share cash drawers, creating unnecessary confusion and accountability concerns. Rather than implementing systems that promote efficiency and accuracy, management seemed more interested in monitoring every movement employees made. Micromanagement was a daily occurrence, frequently accompanied by belittling comments, such as "move faster" that did little to improve performance and instead created an unnecessarily stressful environment.

A particularly disappointing aspect of the culture was the existence of workplace cliques and alliances. Certain employees, many of whom appeared to receive better pay and treatment, routinely spoke down to others with little intervention from management. Respect and professionalism were not applied consistently across the staff. Customers frequently complained of poor treatment from staff, even so far as reporting being called slurs.

The expectations placed on service employees were unreasonable. Workers were expected to take customer orders, maintain a friendly and professional demeanor, sign into the register, process transactions, prepare food on the line, and manage multiple responsibilities simultaneously. Despite already handling numerous tasks, employees were often criticized for not moving quickly enough. The focus seemed to be on creating pressure rather than encouraging productive work.

Scheduling practices also raised concerns. Some employees consistently received consideration for birthdays, anniversaries, graduations, and personal commitments, while others were not afforded the same flexibility. The appearance of favoritism created resentment and undermined morale among staff members who felt their personal obligations were treated as less important.

Another troubling issue was the handling of attendance matters. Management demanded a physician's note for a single-day absence, a response that felt excessive and punitive given the circumstances. 

Rather than generating a reasonable and supportive workplace environment, policies were enforced in a manner that appeared designed to discourage employees from using legitimate time off, including PTO.

Overall, the biggest problem was not the workload itself but the lack of respect, consistency, and sound leadership. Employees were expected to meet exceptionally high standards while receiving little support, unequal treatment, and constant criticism. The result was a workplace culture that felt more focused on control and favoritism rather than teamwork or operational success.
advice: Focus on creating consistent policies, reducing micromanagement, addressing favoritism, and fostering a more respectful and supportive workplace culture.

advice:
Laid off while on disability after 10 months

I joined KFC’s Restaurant Success Center in Plano with 17 years of instructional design experience and was genuinely excited about the opportunity. Ten months later, my position was eliminated while I was out on disability leave.

What makes my experience especially disappointing is that many of the problems I encountered were problems KFC leadership already knew existed.

In an employee meeting discussing results from an internal NPS survey, KFC’s Chief People Officer identified recurring themes employees had raised: workload problems, uncertainty about their future and career development at KFC, “decision friction” caused by difficulty making decisions or decisions later shifting, and inconsistent psychological safety across teams.

Leadership acknowledged that these issues were draining the organization and said KFC needed greater clarity and consistency in leadership, decision-making, and how work gets done.

That description closely matched my experience.

I repeatedly encountered unclear ownership, changing direction, incomplete inputs, fragmented information, compressed timelines, and multiple competing sources of truth. Questions often led to additional folders, systems, documents, search terms or people rather than an authoritative answer. The documented workflow repeatedly required employees to reconstruct the information needed to execute the work.

At one point, after counting five different sources I was expected to consult, I raised the obvious accuracy problem this created. My manager acknowledged that KFC did not always have a single source of truth and said part of the role was cross-referencing the different sources to determine what was correct. She also acknowledged that it was rare to receive a finished source package from which someone could simply execute the work.

That is not how I would normally describe instructional design.

An instructional designer should certainly validate content and collaborate with subject-matter experts. But spending substantial portions of the job on scavenger hunts through Teams, TeamKFC, email, shared drives, live folders and other repositories to determine which version of a fact is actually current is not instructional design expertise. It is compensating for the absence of an effective content-governance process.

KFC was simultaneously emphasizing the need to become more efficient.

I repeatedly tried to create that efficiency by consolidating information, establishing clearer processes, reducing unnecessary sources of truth, clarifying ownership, and defining better handoffs. Those efforts were frequently resisted rather than adopted. The record shows that I identified the multi-channel problem early and attempted to create a consolidated source; that proposed solution was rejected without an alternative centralized system being established.

Eventually these same workflow problems became part of a formal disability-accommodation process.

KFC approved accommodations including clear written instructions, a single source of truth for deliverables and updates, and an escalation path for unmet cross-functional dependencies.

KFC denied two other requested accommodations:

* defined ownership and scope for tasks to reduce ambiguity;
* reasonable timelines aligned to the actual scope of work.

The company checked boxes stating that those requests would be ineffective, would require removal of an essential job function, and would require lowering a performance or production standard.  It also stated that shifting priorities, timelines and deliverables made consistent adherence to the requested accommodations difficult.

That is an extraordinary statement when leadership was simultaneously acknowledging workload problems, decision friction, shifting decisions, and inconsistent ways of working across the organization.

In practice, the “single source of truth” accommodation was also effectively gutted of meaningful enforceability. My manager continued to explain that multiple sources would need to be cross-referenced and that determining which source was correct was simply part of the job.

Which raises a larger question: why did basic good ways of working have to become disability accommodations in the first place?

Clear written direction, one authoritative source for current information, defined ownership, realistic timelines, and an escalation path for blocked work are not exotic requirements. They are ordinary principles of effective knowledge work.

The nature of the actual production work was also surprising.

Despite being hired as an experienced instructional designer, much of my execution was extremely prescriptive and remedial. Rather than being given a business or learning problem and trusted to determine an appropriate solution, I was frequently directed to duplicate existing examples, populate predetermined formats, locate scattered source material, and execute against templates.

I had more creative decision-making authority doing commercial design work in 1995.

For an experienced instructional designer, that is an extraordinary waste of capability. KFC recruited senior professional experience and then used much of it for production activity that allowed very little meaningful instructional or creative judgment.

There were also significant leadership changes during my brief tenure. My manager was later terminated, and ultimately my own position was eliminated while I was on disability leave.

That is particularly difficult to reconcile with the CPO telling employees that people were unsure about their futures and wanted to see a path toward building a long-term career at KFC.

I was recruited as experienced talent. I lasted ten months.

It is not difficult to understand why an organization would struggle when it identifies systemic problems such as workload, decision friction, unclear career paths and psychological safety, yet resists the very process improvements that could address them.

For prospective employees, particularly experienced professionals, I would ask very detailed questions about organizational stability, recent turnover, decision-making authority, workload, psychological safety, content governance, how much autonomy employees actually have to improve broken processes, and how the organization implements disability accommodations in practice rather than merely on paper.

KFC leadership once spoke enthusiastically about the talent the company would be able to attract to Plano.

Attracting talent is only half the equation.

The more important question is whether KFC knows how to use it—or retain it.

summary: Flexible scheduling, but lack of maturity in management
pros: KFC is an employer that I have found allows great flexibility in my schedule as a University Student. At times, I worked with the best team members, made lasting friends, etc.
cons: I've worked here many years, first as a teenager, through to an adult. I don't remember many grown adults running my store, only older teenagers and young twenty-somethings who still hadn't fully matured. I witnessed some questionable workplace expectations, attitudes, and behaviour toward younger staff. I feel they may not have been seen as vulnerable as they were, due to the lack of an age gap with management. In my store, if you were genuinely sick or distressed/overworked for whatever reason, there was no empathy among team members and managers, because they were also forced to work while being sick/overworked/distressed. I began to see this as a very counterproductive mindset in the long term. Then again, while I witnessed many dodgy things while working here, I stayed I felt the benefits to me outweighed the negatives.
advice: After working in another job that shares many similarities with fast-food work, I realised how little effort upper management makes to connect with employees at the bottom end. The only perk is a 20% discount. Still, there are also many other ways to connect with employees, make them feel valued, and make them want to contribute positively toward a fast-food company...

summary: Overwhelming workload and poor communication led to resignation
pros:
* I genuinely enjoyed many of the people I worked with and built strong relationships with employees and other managers.
* Being a GM gave me valuable experience in scheduling, inventory, recruiting, customer service, staffing, and restaurant operations.
* I learned how to operate under pressure and solve problems quickly.
* There were individual managers who cared and tried to help when they could.
cons:
I would not recommend becoming a GM here based on my experience.

As a GM, I routinely worked approximately 65–75 hours per week because my store was severely understaffed. I frequently worked open-to-close shifts, covered call-offs, worked production positions myself, recruited constantly, and completed scheduling, inventory, and other administrative work after closing or from home. I repeatedly communicated to management that I was overwhelmed and needed additional support.

Eventually, I reached the point where I could no longer sustain the workload and resigned as GM. The plan I had been operating under was that I would complete my notice period and then pursue returning as an hourly assistant manager with significantly less responsibility. I was also willing to transfer to another store.

When my MCO needed additional coverage, I agreed to extend my notice by another week to help. During that additional week, I was still communicating with him about the process for returning and asking questions about reapplying.

It was not until my final shift that I was told there were interpersonal concerns and that, rather than returning as an assistant manager, I should take a break and potentially consider reapplying later.

That was my breaking point. I had spent months working extreme hours to keep an understaffed store operational, had already completed my original notice period, and had stayed an additional week specifically to help management with coverage. If I had been told earlier that the expected transition was no longer happening, I could have used that time to pursue other employment instead.

I left that final shift before closing and did not return. Management subsequently classified my separation as involuntary/job abandonment, despite the fact that I had already resigned, completed my original notice period, and was working an additional week beyond it.

Afterward, I contacted HR and upper management multiple times seeking clarification about how my departure had been handled and how my separation had been classified. I did not receive a meaningful response.

The workload itself was difficult enough. What ultimately left the worst impression was the communication and handling of my departure after everything I had done to keep the store operating.
advice:
Develop your new managers instead of only relying on them to keep struggling stores operational.

Most importantly, communicate employment decisions promptly. If someone’s expected transition after resignation is no longer going to happen, tell them as soon as that decision is made. Do not continue accepting additional help from that person and wait until their final shift to communicate the change.

Managers should absolutely be held accountable for their mistakes. Management also has a responsibility to coach people early enough that the feedback can actually help them improve.

summary: Toxic Management Culture at Roseville Galleria
pros: You have a job that pays over minimum wage.
cons:
I’ve worked at the Roseville Galleria location in California for over five years, and I’m making this review because I feel the culture has become increasingly toxic. I’ve tried going through HR in the past, but my experience has been that making a complaint can put a target on your back rather than actually resolving the underlying problem.

In my experience, there are several different management styles at this store. Some managers are genuinely nice but seem more focused on maintaining the status quo than addressing problems. Others are strict and capable of doing their jobs well, but their treatment of employees can depend heavily on their mood. Then there are managers who, in my experience, avoid taking responsibility unless they absolutely have to and push their workload onto captains and other employees.

The last issue has been particularly damaging. Captains are frequently given responsibilities that should be handled by management, which leads to people becoming overwhelmed and eventually leaving. During my time here, I’ve seen the store struggle to retain captains for more than a few months at a time, while store leadership also seems to turn over regularly. In my opinion, this is a symptom of a management culture that has been allowed to continue for years.

Another major problem is how employees are motivated. Praise and constructive feedback can feel rare, while criticism and the threat of disciplinary action or termination are much more common. There also appears to be favoritism at times, whether based on personality, appearance, or which employees a particular manager personally prefers. I have personally benefited from favoritism at times, and I’ve also seen situations where other employees appeared to receive different treatment. That kind of inconsistency creates resentment and makes it difficult for employees to trust management.

My biggest concern is the lack of confidence in the HR process. From my experience, employees can become reluctant to report problems because they worry that management will eventually figure out who made the complaint. When that happens, the employee may feel singled out, micromanaged, or treated as though they are simply being "too sensitive" rather than having their concerns addressed.

After more than five years here, I don't think these are isolated incidents. They feel like recurring management and culture problems that have been allowed to continue for a long time. There are good employees and good managers at this location, but good people can only do so much when the overall management culture doesn't encourage accountability.

If you're considering working here, my advice would be to pay close attention to the specific management team you'll be working under. Your experience can vary significantly depending on who your direct manager is.

summary: "Nordstrom Nice" is a facade - Slow, exclusive, and dated culture
pros:
Predictable Hours: The typical working hours are 9:00 AM to 4:00 PM, and Fridays are exceptionally quiet, with almost no real work being done. If you are looking for a place where you do your hours and log off without high pressure, this fits the bill.

Surface Politeness: People are generally polite on the surface, which keeps day-to-day interactions friction-free.
cons:
The "Hybrid" Lie & Micromanagement: Management brands the role as "hybrid," but forcing people into the office 4 days a week is not hybrid. It’s a thin excuse to micromanage. Even worse, there is a frustrating double standard: I was called out by my manager for arriving at 9:10 AM due to heavy Seattle rain, yet engineers regularly roll in at 10:00 AM without consequence.

The Pointless Commute: They force everyone into the office under the guise of collaboration, but all meetings-even with stakeholders sitting right across the room-are conducted online. You endure a commute for personal interaction, only to sit at your desk on video calls all day.

The "Nordstrom Nice" Illusion: While everyone is superficially friendly, there is zero genuine connection. No one really talks or hangs out during breaks; it is a very insular and isolated environment.

Severe Exclusion of Contractors: There is a toxic division between Full-Time Employees (FTEs) and contractors. You will be explicitly excluded from team bonding. For instance, when a direct team member has a birthday, all the FTEs will leave to celebrate in a separate room, leaving contractors completely uninvited and alienated-even if it's someone you work with side-by-side every day.

Stagnant Culture & Poor Wellness: The demographic composition is completely homogenous, lacking diversity in both backgrounds and perspectives. The office environment leans heavily toward an unhealthy lifestyle, with a pervasive culture centred on fast food (Taco Bell, Dunkin') and sodas at every desk. Even the provided office snacks are exclusively cheap, unhealthy junk food.

Outdated Tech: This is not a cutting-edge tech company. Stagnation is everywhere because the majority of the workforce has been there for 10+ years. People are overly content, comfortable, and slow to adopt new technologies. Innovation and culture makes it feel exactly like a government job.
advice: Stop forcing a 4-day in-office policy to micromanage people onto Teams or Zoom calls all day; if a meeting is in-person, make it in-person; otherwise, let people work from home. Treat contractors like part of the team instead of alienating them from basic workplace celebrations, and address the cultural stagnation by injecting fresh, diverse talent into leadership.

I wasnt even permitted to create a weekly to-do list for all the managers/area supervisors despite it being asked for by those people.
Last thing, the whole place is a massive fire hazard. Im going to be reporting it to the fire marshal because its literally too much to list. Like a wall is crumbling and a dozen go-cart batteries are in carboard boxes in front of the electrical panel.

summary: Great colleagues but overwhelming micromanagement and low pay
pros: Great people to work with on a store level
cons:
I've been with Ross as a Store Manager for quite some time. The company is going through major changes which is a good thing as it needs it. However, due to these changes they are micromanaging field leaders and store leaders to an unbearable level. They expect changes immediately but don't consider how their current payroll model doesn't allow our stores to get ahead. You will always feel behind due to constant payroll cuts as they do not utilize a labor demand model.

Their freight process is outdated, competitor's have palletized freight while we are still having to unload truck using a nestaflex. All merchandise is in cardboard boxes so these boxes (especially in high humidity) tear and fall apart while unloading. The frieght forecast you receive has a margin of error of 20% which is unacceptable as it is detrimental to your payroll. Their frieght scheduling is inconsistent leading you to change your stock teams schedule after you have it posted as they frequently move from 5 days a week to 6 days. This change also impacts you and your leaders as this causes either YOU or your supervisors to work the truck to prevent your stock room lead from hitting OT which places you behind.

The pay for the Associates and supervisors is also laughable. Sales Associates make $11/hr and Supervisors in charge of an entire department make $15/hr. Competitor's offer more per hour and offer a better quality of life working for them. Even outside of their competition scope, you can go be a cashier anywhere else with minimum responsibility and make more money.

HR is a complete JOKE, good luck getting a timely response. They take days to get to you. When they do finally get to you, they then take forever to do an investigation, they ignore your emails for follow ups then they are not aligned with separation and want you to jump through more hoops. So you are now stuck with this low performer causing your high performers to burn out and resign. Did I mention that they still hold YOU accountable for your metrics dropping even though you are doing what you need to do as a leader to damage control?

I cannot recommend this company. Ross is behind the times, while they might have an edge on their competition for reporting sales, the victory won't last long if they do not make changes preemptively. Knowing them, they will wait until its too late and reactivately respond fueling the everyday chaos in the stores.

If you made it this far, I suggest you keep looking for other opportunities as it is not with Ross. They need time to figure out what they doing.
advice: Instead of conducting these "White Glove" visits from senior leadership, actually ask for feedback on how this new direction in impacting the teams running the bottom line. I'd even go as far as suggest undercover boss to see how unrealistic these expectations are especially when the "uncontrollables" completely derail our day to day

summary: Fun work environment, but you'll feel burned out every shift.
pros:
My coworkers are kind and honest. The work is fun when it can be and some of the customers have a good spirit. When it comes to your break, you can at least afford your snacks/meals cause they're cheap. I find it fun to look into what my customers are buying. Managers are great and modest about their greatness. 
Would recommend to a friend because there are worser places to work at.
cons:
Some people have been consistently calling out in my area and I am burnt out from people who don't show up when they're scheduled to. 
If you're a cashier, you only get a ten minute break and it's not enough time for ramen. You'll feel lucky when you get 30 minutes for covering someone else's shift. 
Corporate is dramatic with some of their rules, like it's considered theft if you don't pay for your food, but you require a manager to be present in order to pay for it, and managers can be busy at times. Some customers can be quite impatient whilst making the line longer with demands, especially if they don't calculate their finances whilst shopping. 
Some of the technology is old and when it's broken down, I am told that I am not allowed to put "out of order" signs up.
Some customers don't understand that they should never pay with a $100 bill early in the morning at any store.
If you want to volunteer and do extra work without a payroll, you will be told that you can get written up for it because they have to pay you. 
The trainings on workday are obvious that they're old by many years and have not been updated to match new policies.

summary: Valuable Leadership Experience with Operational Challenges
pros: Working at Dollar Tree provided valuable hands-on leadership experience across every aspect of retail operations. I strengthened my skills in inventory management, merchandising, freight planning, staffing, customer service, compliance, and operational execution. The fast-paced environment challenged me to think quickly, prioritize effectively, and develop my team while delivering results. The relationships I built with my associates and customers were by far the most rewarding part of the job.
cons: The workload often exceeded the labor hours provided, making it challenging to consistently meet operational expectations. Store managers were frequently expected to handle multiple responsibilities while working with lean staffing levels. Facility and equipment issues sometimes took longer than expected to resolve, and support from upper management could be inconsistent. While the job offered valuable experience, maintaining work-life balance could be difficult during peak freight and seasonal periods.
advice: Align expectations with the resources provided. When stores are expected to process large freight volumes, maintain recovery standards, and deliver excellent customer service, they need adequate staffing and labor hours to succeed. Listening to feedback from store-level leaders can help identify practical solutions and improve overall operations.

summary: Great Company but bad management
pros:
Food
Cab
Facilities
Team mates
Learning
cons:
The company itself is actually very good, and I would personally give it 10/10 in many respects. The 1-star rating is specifically because of my experience during the restructuring and internal team-transfer process.

I was part of 7-GT, which was dissolved, and employees had to move to other teams. For some reason, the other teams clearly did not like 7-GT and were reluctant to take people from the team. Because of organizational pressure, they eventually had to accept some of us.

What made the situation ridiculous was that employees were being subjected to 2–4 rounds of interviews just to move to another team within the same organization. This wasn't even for a client project, and there was no hike or salary increase involved. Employees were essentially being interrogated for the privilege of continuing their jobs in another internal team. If we were going to go through that much interviewing anyway, we could have simply interviewed elsewhere and potentially received a 35–60% hike.

During this period, junior employees, SE1s, SE2s, and leads were moved into different teams, while staff-level employees and architects were laid off. The entire process was extremely frustrating and demoralizing.

I personally interviewed with a team called Store Tech, under managers Subhadeep Mondal and Ankit. If your idea of an “Indian manager” is someone with zero respect, questionable technical knowledge, and an ego that is significantly larger than both, then these two are a perfect example.

My interview experience with them was terrible. They came across as arrogant, dismissive, and completely uninterested in listening to the candidate. It felt like they wanted to finish the interview as quickly as possible so they could get back to their tea break. Within the first 10 minutes, I was already 99% certain that I wouldn't be selected—not because of my answers, but because of the way they spoke to and treated me.

I answered approximately 90–95% of their questions correctly. At several points, they tried to convince me that my answers were wrong. I stuck to my answers, later verified them independently, and found that I had been correct.

Despite that, I was rejected approximately five minutes after the interview. I checked with HR and there was apparently no meaningful explanation for the rejection. It didn't even seem like there had been any serious discussion about my candidacy.

Later, after speaking with a few people from their team, I heard similar opinions about these two managers. Based on my own experience, I found them to be arrogant, disrespectful, and unpleasant people to deal with, and I remain baffled by how they ended up in management positions.

Ironically, getting rejected by them turned out to be one of the best things that happened to me. I interviewed elsewhere, received a 40% hike, and left the company.

Unfortunately, not everyone was that lucky. Some of my former colleagues were laid off.

And that's what makes the whole situation particularly frustrating. These managers had an opportunity to take capable employees into their team and potentially help them remain with the organization. Instead, people were rejected through an internal process that often felt arbitrary, while others ultimately lost their jobs.

So, congratulations to Subhadeep Mondal and Ankit: you rejected me, and that rejection helped me get a 40% hike somewhere else.

In hindsight, I should probably thank them.

As for their management style, though: massive ego, little respect, questionable technical depth, and absolutely no sense of how to treat people during an already stressful organizational restructuring. If they ever experience the other side of a layoff themselves, perhaps they'll finally understand what some of the employees they rejected and displaced went through.

Whoever hired them as managers—what exactly were you thinking?

On other note, there were lay off in the company around 12 people or so in 7-GT team alone. But it was step by step and it was not reported anywhere, I could not find anything in linkedinpost or in glassdoor by any of the employees, not sure with what they were threatened with.
advice:
Company should do reviews on Managers, are they capable or not. Most of the managers I met and worked with are 2/10. They believe they know stuffs, in fact all they know is how to smooth talk their superiors. 
Every 6 months an audit should be done on the so called Managers. 7-11 preaches certain principles but non of them are in effect in the organization when it comes to treating the employees.

Consistent schedules are very uncommon for employees.

summary: Results and culture are not separate lanes, they’re one strategy at Wawa.
pros:
What stands out most working for Wawa is how deeply Wawa lives its Six Core Values, especially Valuing People and Doing the Right Thing. The culture genuinely feels like one family, there’s a strong emphasis on respect, recognition, and caring for associates in meaningful ways, not just through words but through daily actions and company-wide programs. That consistency across stores and leaders is what makes the culture feel authentic and enduring. 
Teamwork is built into how we operate. From peer-to-peer recognition through Values nominations to servant leadership practices that encourage leaders to support and serve their teams, collaboration is reinforced daily. 
Leadership support at Wawa is rooted in servant leadership. Leaders are approachable, invested, and focused on helping you grow, not just driving results. There’s a strong balance between accountability and care, with access to coaching, mentorship, and resources that support both personal and professional development. 
Feeling valued comes from trust and recognition. Leaders are empowered to make decisions, develop their teams, and think like owners. Recognition programs, ongoing feedback, and visible investment in leadership development reinforce that store leaders play a critical role in the company’s success. 
Wawa provides continuous growth opportunities through leadership onboarding, formal training, hands-on learning, and movement between stores or regions. These experiences stretch your skills, broaden your perspective, and prepare you for the next level while keeping you challenged and engaged. 
I’m proud that Wawa is a company built around people, not just profits. Whether it’s how we treat our associates, serve our customers, or give back through The Wawa Foundation, there’s a clear commitment to making a positive difference in communities every day.

As a store operations leader, my role directly impacts Wawa’s mission of fulfilling lives every day. By developing strong teams, creating a welcoming environment, and delivering consistent customer experiences, I help bring that mission to life for both associates and customers. 

 If you are looking for a place where people matter, growth is encouraged, and hard work is recognized, Wawa is a great fit. It’s a fast-paced environment, but it’s also one where you’re supported, developed, and truly part of a team. 
Success in store operations comes from adaptability, strong communication, and a genuine commitment to serving others. Leaders who embrace Wawa’s values, stay open to feedback, and focus on developing their people tend to thrive and build strong, successful teams.
cons:
Store operations run 24/7, which can mean long and sometimes unpredictable work hours.
As a 24/7 operation, the role demands flexibility and long hours, especially during peak periods or high T/O staffing challenges.
advice: Focus on developing your people as intentionally as you manage the business; strong teams will always outperform strong managers working alone.

summary: Toxic environment led to resignation
pros: As with any job, your peers are what motivate you.
cons:
Aldi’s Petersburg warehouse engages in behavior that is not just unprofessional — it’s ethically disturbing. I was tasked with “eliminating” the entire ICT team that trained me, which says everything about how disposable people are treated. Leadership also pushed me to terminate a long‑tenured associate before she went out on workers’ comp, and pressured me to get rid of an employee with a known disability by increasing rate demands he physically could not meet.

The conversations behind these decisions were even worse. Leadership openly said things like, “There’s no way **** will be on time every day this week. Attendance is an easy one.” Targeting vulnerable employees — whether through rate, attendance, or timing their termination before medical leave — is disgusting and completely unacceptable.

Turnover among WOSs is out of control. They’ve gone through more than four in under a year, and multiple new hires quit the same day they return from “training” because the environment is that toxic. Training is nonexistent, accountability is zero, and favoritism drives every decision.

Competitive pay cannot justify the unethical practices, hostile culture, and complete lack of integrity inside this building.
advice:
The level of leadership at this facility is shockingly low. I’ve genuinely seen better structure, accountability, and basic professionalism from a nine‑year‑old’s lemonade stand. That’s not sarcasm — it’s an accurate comparison. A child running a sidewalk business shows more consistency, fairness, and integrity than what I witnessed here.

If management wants to fix anything, they need to start with the fundamentals: ethical decision‑making, consistent training, and treating employees like human beings instead of disposable obstacles. Until those basics exist, nothing else will improve

summary: Toxic culture and burnout overshadow high salary
pros: High salary on paper and a car. The store assistants are absolutely amazing in spite of the terrible culture they need to operate in.
cons:
This was genuinely the most traumatising experience of my life. The impact this company has had long term on my self worth is astounding. They operate on a hierarchy built on who is the biggest bully all covered up by wearing posh suits. 

On my first day I was told I had to wear heels and couldn’t have a pink bag, I should’ve turned and ran at that point.

You start your day at 4am to drive to a store they’ve placed you in an hour from where you live. You won’t leave until maybe 9pm at night. I was falling asleep at the wheel to drive home. You will have no work life balance at all. You will work five days a week but on your days off you will be too depressed and tired to do anything.

I was shouted at for sending home a store worker who was crying on the tills because it ‘impacted the sickness KPI’. When I needed surgery I wasn’t able to have any days off and was too scared to ask for sick leave because ‘actions like this will stop you progressing on the graduate scheme’ so I ended up bleeding in the toilets in the store. 

I wish I could say I stormed out and had a final last word but instead they trained me to count stock from the office for speed and then accused me of committing fraud as front for asking me to resign when in actual fact they had hired too many graduates and needed to get rid of some.

I read reviews like this at the time and still chose to go for the job because I was flattered such a well respected scheme wanted me, I IMPLORE you not to do this. There is not a single graduate who started at the same time as me who is still on the scheme because they all get burnt out and realise the salary is not at all proportionate to the hours you work. All the graduates have had to retrain in something else at a significantly lower salary because this job give you no transferable skills (you are a glorified shop assistant). Save yourself some time and pick a scheme that will actually train you up, I promise you’ll make more money in the long run. 

If you do listen to this review - well done, Aldi really don’t deserve you.

If you read this and think ‘that won’t be me’ like I did then I really hope that is the case. As an aside, I found myself sitting reading the exact same Glassdoor reviews a year after I started wishing I’d listened so I’ll see you here in a year.
advice: Truly speechless, nothing will change because the issues flow right from the top. If you are a current Area Manager I advise you attend some external management courses to learn how to behave appropriately at work (and set you up well for your inevitable departure).

pros: I worked here for about two years. The work atmosphere was basically tolerable but there was one hang-up I experienced with the location of cleaning equipment to clean up aisle spills and such.

Safeway's online schedule system for employees which is supposed to be accessible via Safeway's corporate website (it was not an app they had been using back then) often refused to deliver my work schedule in a true machine-readable format, as well. The site often would not let me log on using my Safeway-provided credentials. This was highly irritating for me. When I asked this Corvallis Safeway store's management if they could request that Safeway HQ fix this problem with their software and its scheduling they would never follow up with me or recognize what I had to say as a valid concern. Several people, mostly the cashiers, called this store Slaveway. What I do vividly remember is that I had a true problem  getting scheduling started and finished online: for example setting my hours and also setting my preferences for the available work shifts. Someday they must fix this scheduling snafu and also raise their darn wages.

summary: Friendly environment overshadowed by poor upper management and false promises
pros: Friendly environment and great co-workers. Being a floral clerk was hands down my favorite customer service job I've worked. Made some nice friends working there, and the stress of work was easily handled because of the friendly people.
cons:
Seniority was definitely a thing. I was expected to take shifts that the other people didn't want until someone newer came along, and then I had seniority over them.

Upper management for the store was also the worst. They would take credit for our department's hard work and shift blame onto us for oversights or actions on their part. Once I got promoted to admin, I saw how little they cared about their employees. They would make passing comments and openly admit to giving certain employees who were "problem people" bad shifts or deny their requests for days off. I was in charge of making the schedule and would be told not to give certain people the days they wanted that week, even if they were within their availability, just to make things difficult for them.

They also don't promote from within. I was asked to be the interim manager when our manager went on maternity leave. I stepped up and took on manager duties despite not getting a pay raise. When my manager decided she wanted to move stores, she was hoping I would be given the role permanently. Instead, they decided to bring in someone from another store, and I had to train her to be a floral manager at ours.

They did eventually promote me to store admin, but my passion was working in floral. I agreed on the promotion as long as I could still work in the floral department, but they eventually phased me out of that role. Literally tricked me into taking a promotion and then falling back on the terms we agreed on.
advice: It doesn't take much out of your day to help people out. Maybe understand that everyone in the store is doing their best. Uplift your employees rather than make their time at work difficult, and these "problem people" might actually step up and help you out when you need.

pros:
Floral was genuinely one of my most fulfilling jobs. My manager at downtown Renton really helped me understand what I needed to know and was super kind and understanding. I'd work there again if I ever got the chance
Grocery department was also super helpful to me when it could be, they were patient and kind with my first job experience.
Cashiering usually had me end up in the SwS. Either way I never had an issue and management was usually pretty on top of things. The wage was fantastic and really felt like I could afford to live somewhere someday. Which is a rare find.
Some employees take a bit to warm up to but most were super kind and I'd argue eventually all of them are, at downtown Renton. I had such a good experience working with everyone I met and it actually broke my heart when I had to leave. I felt like I made good connections with everyone.
cons:
I dont have a lot, but when the store got busy and I couldn't get a key to unlock our alcohol section it really held things up. [I can 
understand this was more of a trust thing, but it hurt my efficiency and i would be looked at for not being fast enough]. Getting a manager override to void a transaction or remove an item someone no longer wants or I may have overscanned by mistake also caused huge backups in the line. Still not sure why I needed someone just to stop a transaction.
Sometimes I was one of two cashiers on duty if that during peak hours. Someone would step in to help sometimes but it was infrequent.
Infrequently customers would be annoyed with me for things impossibly out of my control, such as not getting the correct items on a sale or a sale out of date that wasn't removed. Rather than explaining to the customer the options available they'd give the discount anyway as to not deal with it and I feel as though that hurt the customers experience with me in my opinion. It wasn't that bad, but it always sticks with me.
Some customers in the area are genuinely abusive. This isn't anything about staff but thats something to note about just the general area and something to note.
Floral dept. to me did not have downsides that I can think of.
advice: Not much, just maybe when sales are expired or not for the correct item explain thats why the cashier was trying to deny a coupon? It was never consistent.

summary: Enterprise-London
pros:
Enterprise is a company where you control your progression and advancement .They reward hard work in  all aspects of the business.You get what you put in with Enterprise .Each customer transaction is your own to control ,weather it be finding the perfect car for that customer or advising them on certain products we offer .Within the company you get a taste for all different elements of the business such as customer service , sales , marketing , fleet growth  and much more .Enterprise is a fun and friendly place to work , the buzz is great and moral is always high .Sales and service games keeps everyone on their toes as well as keeping energy levels high at all times during a shift.Opportunities are endless in regards to career progression at Enterprise , you are a manager in training when join  Enterprise and your path is clearly laid out in front of you from day 1 .

Airport branches differ from city branches but both have their benefits.Day in each would consist of a morning meeting with all staff on shift that day.In the meeting managers and staff will discuss goals for the day,acknowledge positives from anyone present , delegate tasks and speak about reservations for the day.Throughout the day you will build rapport with customers and assist them throughout their rental agreement.In city and local branches you will get the opportunity to go and pick up customers and bring them to your branch (once your probation is up).Admin duties are completed throughout the day and consist of follow up calls,reservation confirmation and and issues customers may have with their rental.Before you know it your day is  done . 

On a personal note I joined Enterprise on a placement with University and loved every minute .I loved the teamwork , the working environment and opportunities that the company offered.I am now back at Enterprise picking up exactly where I left off and continuing my journey to becoming a manger.

So if you like a challenge , your driven ,your not afraid to roll your sleeves up now and again and your ambitious , Enterprise is 100 percent the place for you !
cons:
The hours at Enterprise can be challenging but as is with any customer service based roll in today's business environment .There is opportunity for overtime of course and is paid .

If you have not got any previous experience in customer service you may find it daunting at first but I assure you it is the best company to gain this experience from.

summary: High pay, but politics and constant pressure have ruined morale and culture
pros:
- pretty high pay
- monthly vesting for RSUS
- ESPP
- 401k matching
- WLB not bad depending on team
- Yearly refreshers and Bonus
cons: eng culture specifically has turned into a political game of who can put up the most diffs and ERDs.  You are now stack ranked amongst your peers and put into PIP, does not meet bar, bar, above expectations, and exceeds expectations.  Know now that the above expectations and exceeds expectations is exceptionally rare and the percentage allowed in that bucket is very very low.  Over the past two years the more people put on PIP and in the does not meet expectations requirements has increased a lot.  Without warning too really.  Have seen good people put in the does not meet expectations who are actually the smartest and team leads.  And what’s the reason for it?  Oh you are below on diff count for X amount of months, surely that means you’re slacking on your velocity.  Oh you only wrote on ERD over past couple months.  I don’t care that it is 50 pages and is one of the biggest projects on the team.  You clearly don’t have enough impact if you only delivered one of the most major projects on the team, you have to deliver 5 or 6 projects per half minimum.  That’s the name of the game now.  You’ll see everyone, from people who coast to even the smartest people in the company, put up code changes that are essentially just one liner log or metric changes and go around begging teammates for stamps just so they can hit their diff count at the end of the month.  What does this accomplish?
advice: Remove this productivity metric tracking nonsense and using it as a core benchmark for performance.  It just ruins morale and stops actual meaningful work from being done.  I’ve seen most of the good engineers in my org leave the company because of this.

summary: Lyft’s pricing is deceptive and feels like a classic bait-and-switch.
pros: There is nothing good about lyft
cons: Lyft’s pricing is deceptive and feels like a classic bait-and-switch.
advice:
Lyft’s pricing is deceptive and feels like a classic bait-and-switch.

I originally booked an Uber, but I canceled it because I had a $10 Chase Sapphire ride credit that I wanted to use with Lyft.

When I booked my Lyft ride from my residence to Tampa International Airport, the app clearly showed the fare as $36.98. At that point, I hadn’t even entered my Chase Sapphire card information yet, so that quoted price could not have included the $10 Chase credit.

After I reserved the ride, Lyft placed a temporary authorization charge on my credit card for $36.98, confirming that this was the fare I had agreed to.

However, after the ride was completed, Lyft billed me $46.98. Only after the $10 Chase Sapphire credit was applied did my final out-of-pocket cost become $36.98—the exact price Lyft had displayed before I ever added my payment method.

In other words, the advertised fare wasn’t the actual fare at all. Lyft effectively increased the ride price by $10 and then used my Chase credit to bring it back down to the original quoted amount. That isn’t a discount—it’s misleading pricing that deprives customers of the benefit of their credit.

Displaying one price to get customers to book a ride and then charging a higher fare after the ride is completed is deceptive and undermines trust. If the actual fare is $46.98, that’s the price Lyft should display upfront. Customers shouldn’t discover after the fact that a third-party credit merely offsets an undisclosed price increase.

This experience has completely eroded my confidence in Lyft’s pricing transparency, and unless this billing practice changes, I won’t be using or recommending the service.
